source: Silver et al. (2017) Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General RL Algorithm (AlphaZero)
finding: AlphaZero learned chess from the rules only, by self-play, and beat Stockfish. It used MCTS guided by a network instead of alpha-beta.
numbers: 100-game match vs Stockfish: 28 wins, 72 draws, 0 losses (as White 25W 25D 0L; as Black 3W 47D 0L). Beat Stockfish after 4 hours (300k steps). 5,000 TPUs for self-play, 64 TPUs to train. Searches 80k positions/s vs Stockfish 70M/s.
quote: AlphaZero compensates for the lower number of evaluations by using its deep neural network to focus much more selectively
limits: Stockfish ran at 1 min/move, 64 threads, 1GB hash; this setup was later disputed. Self-play needs a perfect simulator and huge compute.
agent_relevance: Learned guidance lets a search look at about 1000x fewer nodes. Pruning by a good prior beats brute width.

source: Silver et al. (2017) AlphaZero, scaling with thinking time
finding: AlphaZero MCTS gained more Elo per extra thinking time than alpha-beta in Stockfish and Elmo. This questioned the belief that alpha-beta is inherently better.
numbers: Figure 2: Elo vs thinking time, relative to Stockfish/Elmo at 40 ms; AlphaZero scaled better in chess and shogi.
limits: Read off a figure; no per-doubling number in text. Single lab, own hardware.
agent_relevance: Search budget is a dial, and the value of extra budget depends on how good the guide is. Spend S6 budget only where the guide is good.

source: Schrittwieser et al. (2020) MuZero
finding: MuZero plans with a learned model and is not given the rules. It matched AlphaZero in chess, shogi and Go and set a new state of the art on 57 Atari games.
numbers: 800 simulations per search in board games, 50 in Atari. Matched superhuman AlphaZero Elo without the rules.
limits: Still needs huge self-play. Reward must be scalar.
agent_relevance: Search over a learned world model, not the true one. An LLM agent's S6 search is also over a learned, imperfect model, so value errors compound.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Adversarial Policies Beat Superhuman Go AIs
finding: Adversary policies trained against KataGo won by tricking it into blunders, not by playing Go well. Human experts copied the strategy and beat superhuman Go AIs.
numbers: Win rate >99% vs KataGo with no search; >97% vs KataGo at superhuman settings; adversary used under 14% of KataGo training compute; victim searches 10M nodes/move in one setting. Still worked against 10^7-visit victims.
quote: even superhuman AI systems may harbor surprising failure modes
limits: Go-specific blind spot; victim is a fixed known program.
agent_relevance: Deep search plus self-play does not remove blind spots. Search cannot find errors the evaluator cannot see; keep an independent check (G3).

source: Jones (2021) Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games
finding: With AlphaZero on Hex, compute needed rises predictably with board size. Train-time compute and test-time search compute trade off.
numbers: For each extra order of magnitude of train-time compute, test-time compute can drop by a similar factor with performance unchanged.
quote: for each extra order of magnitude of train-time compute, we can reduce test-time compute by a similar factor
limits: Hex only, small boards, AlphaZero-style agents.
agent_relevance: Early precedent for LLM test-time compute work: search at inference can buy back training. Scale S6 budget with problem size.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts, Game of 24
finding: A search loop (BFS or DFS over LLM-proposed thoughts, scored by the LLM) around GPT-4 hugely raised Game of 24 success.
numbers: GPT-4 Game of 24: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC k=100 9.0%, IO best-of-100 33%, CoT best-of-100 49%, IO+Refine 27%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%.
quote: ToT with a breadth of b = 1 already achieves a success rate of 45%, while b = 5 achieves 74%
limits: Short, checkable steps. Thought scoring is by the same LLM. GTBench (c13) finds ToT does not always help.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for tree search at S6. Best-of-100 CoT reaches 49%, so the gain over plain sampling at matched cost is smaller than the headline 4% vs 74%.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts, cost and ablation
finding: The paper compares ToT against best-of-k at equal nodes visited, and shows that pruning is what helps. A weaker generator (GPT-3.5) with ToT scores far lower.
numbers: GPT-3.5 + ToT 19% vs GPT-4 + ToT 74% on Game of 24 (ablation table).
limits: Many more tokens per task than CoT. Tested on three tasks only.
agent_relevance: Search needs a good scorer and generator; weak model plus ToT stays weak.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: RAP uses the LLM as both world model and policy, searched with MCTS. It lifted Blocksworld sharply over CoT with the same LLaMA-33B.
limits: Blocksworld has a crisp state; the LLM simulates it reliably on small problems. Gain on GSM8K is smaller.
agent_relevance: Restating and simulating the state before choosing is what search needs. Supports a state-tracking check in S6.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: LATS runs MCTS over agent trajectories with an LLM value function and self-reflection, using real environment feedback.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 GPT-3.5: CoT 46.9, ReAct 56.9, Reflexion 68.1, ToT 54.4, RAP 63.1, LATS 83.8. GPT-4: base 80.1, Reflexion 91.0, LATS 92.7. Settings: n=5 expansions, 8 iterations (code); n=5, k=50 (HotpotQA).
limits: Gain over Reflexion with GPT-4 is 1.7 points. Many more model calls. Gains lean on real execution feedback.
agent_relevance: Search that touches real test output (G2, G3) works; search on model opinion alone is weaker.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) ReST-MCTS*
finding: MCTS guided by process rewards inferred from final-answer correctness gave better traces for self-training than best-of-N and ToT at the same search budget.
numbers: Abstract claims higher accuracy than Best-of-N and ToT under the same budget; exact table not extracted this session.
limits: Needs ground-truth final answers to infer step rewards. Numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Search yields training signal as well as answers, but needs an oracle label.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) Planning with LLMs for Code Generation (PG-TD)
finding: MCTS over token decoding, with public test cases as the reward, beat beam search and sampling for code.
numbers: Abstract: higher pass rates than baselines on APPS and CodeContests with several backbones; exact figures not extracted.
limits: Reward is the test pass rate, i.e. real execution.
agent_relevance: Another case where tree search works because the leaf evaluator is external and exact.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally
finding: The best way to spend test-time compute depends on prompt difficulty. Search against a process reward model helps on harder items; revision helps on easier ones.
numbers: Compute-optimal strategy gives more than 4x efficiency over best-of-N; in FLOPs-matched tests a small model with test-time compute beats a 14x larger model where base success is non-trivial.
limits: Math only; PRM trained for it. On the hardest items extra compute does little.
agent_relevance: Adaptive budget per question fits G1: spend search only when signals say the item is hard.

source: Gao et al. (2024) GTBench: Strategic Reasoning of LLMs via Game-Theoretic Tasks
finding: Across 10 games, LLMs fail in complete-information deterministic games but compete in probabilistic ones. CoT and ToT do not always help; code pretraining helps.
numbers: 10 tasks; LLM vs LLM and vs MCTS agents; GPT-4 and Llama-3-70B lead open models; 157 turns hand-checked in error analysis (50 matches x 5 turns).
quote: advanced reasoning methods such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Tree-of-Thought (ToT) do not always help
limits: Prompt-only play, no engine. Exact normalised scores not extracted.
agent_relevance: Prompted tree-of-thought is not a reliable stand-in for a real search loop run by code.

source: Toshniwal et al. (2022) Chess as a Testbed for Language Model State Tracking
finding: Transformers trained on chess move strings learn to track pieces and predict legal moves when data is large. Small data needs board-state supervision, and full attention to history is needed.
numbers: Three findings: (a) high legal-move accuracy with enough data; (b) board-state supervision helps on small data; (c) approximating full attention drops performance significantly. Exact percentages not extracted.
limits: Trained from scratch on chess text, not a general chat LLM.
agent_relevance: State tracking is a prerequisite for search; give the model the board explicitly rather than the move history.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent World Models and Latent Variable Estimation in Chess-Playing Language Models
finding: A GPT trained on chess PGN text shows linear board-state probes and plays well. Adding a player-skill vector raised win rate.
numbers: Legal move rate 99.8% (16-layer), 99.6% (8-layer). Win rate vs Stockfish 16 level 0 (about 1300 Elo): 46% (8-layer), 64% (16-layer). Best board probe accuracy 99.6%. Skill-vector intervention: win rate up to 2.6x.
limits: Small custom model; one Stockfish level; Elo mapping approximate.
agent_relevance: The model estimates player skill from context, so a prompt implying a strong player may change play.

source: Feng et al. (2023) ChessGPT
finding: Fine-tuning on chess game and language data greatly improved state tracking over general LLMs.
numbers: BigBench chess state tracking: LLaMA-7B 29.5% / 39.3% / 53.0% (real short/med/long); ChessGPT-Base 99.5 / 97.7 / 98.1. Synthetic: LLaMA 31.3 / 39.9 / 45.8 vs ChessGPT-Base 94.2 / 94.6 / 92.8.
limits: 7B models, not frontier. State tracking is not play strength.
agent_relevance: General LLMs track boards poorly without domain data; a code-held board object is safer.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess
finding: A 270M transformer trained to imitate Stockfish 16 action values plays at grandmaster level with no search.
numbers: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 vs humans; ChessBench: 10M games, 15 billion annotated data points; the Stockfish action-value oracle corresponds to Elo 2713.
limits: Distillation is imperfect; weaker than Stockfish. Blitz Elo vs humans.
agent_relevance: Search can be distilled into a net, but only after heavy engine-labelled training that a scaffold lacks.

source: Schultz et al. (2024) Mastering Board Games by External and Internal Planning with Language Models
finding: A language model (MAV) trained as policy, world model and value, placed inside MCTS, reached grandmaster chess without an engine. Internal search (tree written in context) was also trained.
numbers: Chess external Elo 2923 (mean scoring), 2875 (max scoring). MAV-MCTS with 100 simulations gave +68 internal Elo over searchless MAV; Elo grows roughly logarithmically with simulations. Connect Four: at least +244 Elo. Games played: 14,689 chess, 4,480 Chess960, 2,189 Connect Four, 6,334 Hex.
quote: search-based planning can yield significant improvements in LLM game-playing strength
limits: Heavy domain pretraining; model must emit legal move and next FEN reliably. Not a generic LLM. Elo anchored to CCRL blitz.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that LLM-guided MCTS gives log-linear gains, so cap simulations.

source: Campbell, Hoane, Hsu (2002) Deep Blue
finding: Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997 by brute-force alpha-beta search on custom chips with a hand-tuned evaluation.
numbers: 1997 match 3.5-2.5; about 200 million positions per second (from memory, not opened).
limits: From memory this session.
agent_relevance: Brute force needed special hardware; an LLM agent cannot afford it, so selectivity matters.

source: Silver et al. (2016) Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search
finding: AlphaGo combined policy and value networks with MCTS.
numbers: From memory: beat Fan Hui 5-0; beat Lee Sedol 4-1 in 2016. Not opened.
limits: From memory.
agent_relevance: A value net replaces random rollouts; the analogue is an LLM verifier.

source: Kocsis & Szepesvari (2006) Bandit based Monte-Carlo Planning (UCT)
finding: UCT treats each tree node as a bandit and gives a regret bound for MCTS.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: From memory.
agent_relevance: Rule for which thought branch to expand at S6; links to the bandit-exploration subfield.

source: Knuth & Moore (1975) An analysis of alpha-beta pruning
finding: Alpha-beta gives the same value as minimax while visiting about the square root of the nodes under best move ordering.
numbers: Best case about b^(d/2) nodes. Not opened.
limits: From memory.
agent_relevance: Ordering of candidates decides how much pruning you get; a model that ranks thoughts well makes search cheap.

source: Carlini (2023) Playing chess with large language models (blog)
finding: Reported that gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct plays chess far better than chat-tuned models, which often make illegal moves.
numbers: About 1750 Elo estimate (from memory, not opened).
limits: Blog, not peer reviewed; prompt format (PGN continuation) mattered. Unverified.
agent_relevance: Prompt format moved play strength more than any reasoning scaffold; test format first.

source: Kaggle / Google DeepMind Game Arena LLM chess tournament (2025)
finding: Public LLM vs LLM chess tournament; reports of illegal moves and blunders even in top models.
numbers: Details not opened; unverified.
limits: Unverified.
agent_relevance: Cite only after reading.

source: Stockfish NNUE and Leela Chess Zero (2020-2024) engine designs
finding: Strongest engines either pair alpha-beta with a small learned evaluation (Stockfish NNUE) or MCTS with a transformer policy (Lc0). Neither design is clearly dominant.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: From memory.
agent_relevance: Proven recipe is fast narrow search plus learned evaluation.

source: Comparison of c17 (Ruoss 2024) and c18 (Schultz 2024)
finding: Two routes reach about 2900 Elo: distil search into a feed-forward net (2895) or put a small search around a language model (2923 mean scoring).
numbers: c17: 2895 (Lichess blitz, vs humans). c18: 2923 (CCRL blitz anchored). Anchors differ, so not strictly comparable.
limits: Paper warns external Elos are anchored to CCRL Blitz.
agent_relevance: Search is partly replaceable by amortised knowledge, but a prompt-only scaffold has no such training.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Go adversaries, defence result
finding: Patching KataGo against the first adversary did not close the hole; a second cyclic adversary was trained after the patch.
numbers: Earlier work (Timbers et al.) got 90% win rate vs no-search AlphaZero and 65% at 800 visits; this attack beat a 10^7-visit victim. Defence win-rate details not extracted.
limits: Details of the defence experiments not read closely.
agent_relevance: Fixing one blind spot with more search or training does not remove the class; keep independent checks.
